newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: First S.Africa offshore oil now expected mid-March.
newsitem.headline: First S.Africa offshore oil now expected mid-March.

text.p: South African state-owned oil exploration company Soekor E&P expects to start producing its first offshore oil by mid-March, a month later than initially expected, chief executive Joggie Heuser said on Monday.
"The refurbishing of the rig has fallen slightly behind schedule and the shipyard work should now be completed in early January 1997," Heuser told Reuters.

The rig, the Orca, is being refurbished in Simon's Town and was originally due to be ready to move to the Oribi oilfield off Mossel Bay by the end of November with oil production commencing in February.
But bad weather delayed the erection of scaffolding and the mooring system was damaged several times hampering operations on deck, Heuser said.

Heuser said that during the refurbishment, overseen by lead contractor Schlumberger Logelco Inc, the storage/shuttle tanker on the rig had been upgraded, modified and fully certified at Keppel Shipyard in Singapore.
The rig was due to undergo sea trials in False Bay before leaving for Mossel Bay and these would be audited by the American Bureau of Shipping to certify the upgrading and refurbishment work.
"The rig should leave Simon's Town harbour by mid-January...," Heuser said.
The rig would initially have about 90 people on board, reduced to 35 once oil started pumping.

The crewing of the rig was part of the overall contract with Schlumberger Logelco Inc and Fred Olsen Production of Norway to develop the oil field and they have sourced people internationally and locally.
The project will involve the re-entry and completion of three existing wells with a network of connections to the rig, which has been customised to serve as a floating production vessel.

The Oribi oilfield is expected to initially produce 20,000 barrels of oil a day, with this amount tapering off over three to six years. It will form the nucleus for the subsequent development of several other nearby oil discoveries, which would extend production life by a further six years.
Eighty percent of the project's $75 million capital costs have been met by syndicated foreign loans and the full capital cost of the project is expected to be recovered within a year of operation.

Soekor and its 20 percent partner, Energy Africa Ltd, plan to pump the oil into a one million barrel shuttle tanker for shipment to one of South Africa's three coastal refineries in Cape Town or Durban.
